Phil Tippett INTERVIEW BY JOE FORDHAM pantheon of creatures greets visitors to the Tippett Studio effects facility in Berkeley, California. Die-hard fans might recognize the holographic chess set from Star Wars or the shovel-nosed ED-209 from RoboCop. Venture further in and Draco, the mythological star of Dragonheart, resides beside a colorful menagerie of alien lifeforms from Evolution. Ray the dancing guinea pig and Carl the rabbit from the Blockbuster Video television commercials point the way upstairs, past a miniature T-rex from Jurassic Park to an office where a tiny mechanical AT-AT Imperial snowwalker sits as a relic from The Empire Strikes Back. Seated in the office is Phil Tippett, creative father to many of the characters on display. In a 27-year career that
Q&A: Phil Tippett

has bridged the gap between the tactile manipulations of stop-motion animation to modern digital 3D character animation - seen most recently in Blade II, The Matrix Revolutions and Hellboy - Tippett has earned two Academy Awards and two Emmys. Continuing the tradition of character-driven dimensional animation exemplified by effects guru Ray Harryhausen, a friend of many years, Tippett and partners Jules Roman and Craig Hayes oversee a staff of more than 200, and have 43 features to their credit. But while his company is among the top-rung computer animation facilities, Tippett retains an antipathy for the industry's technical trappings - a stance that is succinctly trumpeted in the studio's tongue-in-cheek T-shirt catchphrase: 'Creativity or Death.' "I'm just a film buff," Tippett asserted. "I don't even know how to turn the bloody computer on. I don't know, and I don't want to know!" Tippett's creative journey has most recently led him to direct his first feature film with the direct-to-video release, Starship Troopers 2: Hero of the Federation - the sequel to director Paul Verhoeven's science fiction blockbuster, which in 1997 earned Tippett his sixth Academy Award nomination. Graced with a $7 million budget - compared to the original's $95 million - Starship Troopers 2 proved to be a trial by fire. Tippett lived to tell the tale and took time to reflect on the state of How long was Starship Troopers 2 in development? About a year and a half ago, producer Jon Davison went to Screen Gems to determine if there was any feasibility in doing a low-budget, direct-to-video Starship Troopers. Because Troopers was part of its franchise, Screen Gems was interested - as long as it could be done for between five and seven million dollars, and not a penny more. When the studio agreed to give us autonomy in putting the movie together, without anyone second-guessing us, it became an attractive thing to do. And so, screenwriter Ed Neumeier and I rented a little house on the beach in Marin for a weekend and banged out the story. Was your story based on any of Robert Heinlein's original source material? No, we didn't stay with the Heinlein story. Instead, we took the universe of the first Starship Troopers theatrical feature, which was in the nature of a war picture, and went from there. The idea was that if the action in Starship Troopers had been the equivalent of World War II, the battle with the bugs had been going on for maybe twelve years and had rolled into the equivalent of Korea or Vietnam. So the characters had gotten past the nationalism and all the hoopla, and had become more realistic about what it meant to be fighting all 16 • CINEFEX 97 the time. Among the Heinlein concepts dropped from the first film were the 'Skinnies' - the Arachnid's humanoid alien allies - and the mechanized power suits worn by the Federation infantry. Did you consider resurrecting any of those elements for Starship Troopers 2? No. The Skinnies and the power suits would have been huge budgetary issues. For our budget, it was clear that what we had to do was make a horror picture. If Starship Troopers was analogous to Aliens, then Starship Troopers 2 was the equivalent of Alien - a 'dark old house' story with people getting killed. So, no space battles? We couldn't afford space! The space ships at the beginning of the film are stock shots from the first film that Sony let us have. In the original film there were six types of alien Arachnids. Do all of them make a reappearance in Starship Troopers 2? Only the Warrior Bugs made it back - though two new breeds of bugs show up: Spy Bugs and Parasite Bugs. We had done a number of iterations on these two new bug characters, but they weren't working out. So, as a friend, my longtime associate, Craig Hayes - who had designed the bugs on the first Starship Troopers - agreed to help us out. He came up with some really terrific designs for the Spy Bugs and Parasite Bugs. I understand there were no animatronic bugs on set. What role did physical effects play in the production? Michael Lantieri and his guys did all our floor effects, and they were tremendous contributors to the film. Without Michael, we couldn't have done the show. His crew took care of explosions, electrical sparks, blood effects, wind, fire, smoke, fog - and we had physical effects working all the time. Michael really saved our butts. A few years ago, you helped Michael on his directorial debut, Komodo. Did Michael have any words of wisdom, from the point of view of having been an effects man - albeit a different kind of effects man - making a transition to directing? He did, by virtue of saying, ¿Just tell me what you want, and I'll do it." He knew from having been there that he didn't want to hassle us. We told him what we wanted and he did a terrific job. What influenced your decision to shoot on highdefinition video? Because we were going direct to video anyway. The premise was that we would be able to get into the computer more efficiently. The HD cameras did give us a higher-resolution image, but it was tricky. The technology is still run by the rocket scientists, and hasn't been worn in by the artists yet. All digital imagery has a tendency to look flat and electronic, so making the imagery

The Arachnids of planet Zulu Angel menace a lost Federation patrol in Starship Troopers 2: Hero of the Federation, a direct-to-video sequel to director Paul Verhoeven's science fiction blockbuster. Starship Troopers 2 marked the directorial debut of Phil Tippett, who had served as creature visual effects supervisor on the 1997 original. His work on that first film had earned him a sixth Academy Award nomination and established Tippett Studio as a leader in the field of digital character animation. look good became a huge issue. We solved it primarily by using lots of smoke. How did the HD format influence your choices of color palette and contrast? We had a good relationship with Franco-Giacomo, the production designer, who gave everything a very muted palette. George Lucas always said he wanted a 'used future' for Star Wars. Ours was an abused future! Everything on our planet was corroded and falling apart, so we had a lot of rust and concrete surfaces. We wanted everything to feel as if it had weight and mass. The problem with a lot of science fiction pictures is that everything has to feel as if it's made out of chrome - but the sets and props are always made out of vacuform styrene, so they look phony. How many days did you shoot? Twenty-six days! Everybody said it was going to be horrible, and it was. All the departments came through and the cast was very helpful - but it was brutal. We worked around the clock, returning to work just six hours after wrap each day. Fortunately, I had a very experienced first assistant director, Mark Little, who kept us all on track. We also couldn't have gotten through the 26 days without Ed Neumeier. He was with us the entire time, and at the end of every 12- or 18-hour day, we spent two or three hours together, preparing for the next day. We had some horrible moments. The way they make these pictures, the studio enlists a bond company, which reviews your shooting schedule and projects if the picture is going over budget. And if it does go over budget, the bond company takes over. We had all our huge battle scenes in the first week of shooting; and by the end of that week I was two and a half days over schedule. The bond company told us that if we didn't want to be taken over, we had to lose the equivalent time from our script. So I had to cut ten pages out of the script - and it wasn't a long script to begin with, just 95 pages. It was like chopping off my fingers! But we learned the lesson that we couldn't go over schedule; and we shot everything as quickly as possible. I remembered watching Spielberg shoot Jurassic Park. Very early on, because of the budgetary constraints on that film, he had shot in what he called 'Clint Eastwood style' - which meant two takes and then he moved on. For this, we couldn't even shoot Clint Eastwood style! They ended up calling me 'One Take Tippett.' I had to move that fast, just to get it all done. How did that influence your shooting style? We shot with two cameras to get extra coverage, and there was a tremendous amount of hand-held work. Did you use any motion control for visual effects? CINEFEX 97 ~ 17

We had carefully limited the number of moving camera shots; but I fell into the trap that all the directors I have worked for fall into - when you're shooting, a lot of times you just push on and ignore the plan. But we had pretty rigorously storyboarded not only the visual effects scenes but all the major body of the story, so I had a place to start. Did you do any 3D previsualization? Yes, that was one of the advantages of having the resources of our studio. We had so much time ramping up and there was a little bit of downtime at our studio, so our animation supervisor Pete Konig and Blair Clark did quite a bit of previsualization. Other than Spielberg, were there other directors who informed your shooting choices? Paul Verhoeven was very much my mentor on this picture. I touched base with him quite a bit to discuss practicalities of the approach. He's done mostly biggerbudget pictures here in the States, but he started off doing lower-budget pictures, and he helped me strategize getting through the day. Robert Altman was also an influence. He has an atypical approach to acting, where the actors do not wait for their closeups to turn in a performance. Since we had two cameras going all the time, everybody was in character all the time because they never knew if the B-camera might pick up 18 • CINEFEX 97 their performance. How did you work with the actors? Have you done that before? Not to this degree. My skill as an acting coach is absolutely nil! My general approach was to spend a tremendous amount of time hiring and interviewing people, because it's all about the casting, as they say. I also asked Jon Davison for three days of rehearsal. Jon's response was: 'You want to rehearse on this budget? I've never rehearsed anything!' What, specifically, did you want to accomplish in the rehearsal period? I wanted the performers to have some combat training. A Marine drill instructor spent a day with the actors, putting them in military mode. We spent another day working out action choreography; and we spent a day discussing what happens to a number of characters that become infected and turn into zombies. I wanted to get another coat of paint on that concept so it wouldn't be like The Night of the Living Dead or other films we've seen before. We wanted a different feeling, as though these characters had been hijacked against their will. Beyond that, my directions to the actors were: 'You have carte blanche. You create the characters. It's there on the page. Ed wrote it; you run with it; I'll shoot it.' After that, it was just a matter of making adjustments in terms Tippett's early work included animation of the tauntauns seen scampering across the ice planet Hoth in the opening act of The Empire Strikes Back. Achieved entirely with practical, frame-byframe manipulation of physical models, and optically composited into miniature and live-action settings, the tauntauns and a subsequent snow battle featuring giant, lumbering war machines were a bold extension of Tippett's first stop-motion work at Industrial Light & Magic - the holographic chessmen for Star Wars.

Tippett attends to Vermithrax Perjorative and a tiny puppet representing Peter MacNichol astride the creature's neck for the finale of the 1981 fantasy, Dragonslayer. The ILM project earned Tippett his first Oscar nomination and showcased the computer-assisted stop-motion technique, 'go-motion?' Developed for animating tauntauns and used through the 1980s, the process allowed animators to manipulate puppets via servo-driven rods, producing frame-by-frame motion blur that eliminated the strobing of traditional stop-motion.Advancing technology relegated the process to a historical curiosity. of timing and choreography. After the difficult shoot, were you happy to get into the postproduction process? Yeah. I was safe again, back in my garret, working with people I knew. My big fear, at that point, was that I hadn't shot enough to put it all together. Some things did slip through the cracks, either through lack of time or through inexperience. But one of the tremendous assets of shooting digitally, particularly on a schedule like this, was the ability to take a shot, digitally enlarge it, and reframe it. I took a ton of shots and recomposed them - sometimes taking wide master shots and turning them into medium shots. Louise Rubacky, the editor, and I did a lot of fixes in post that got us out of jams. Your visual effects supervisor, Eric Leven, mentioned that the postproduction schedule for Troopers 2 was 30 percent more work, with 50 percent less crew and 1/16 of the budget of the first Starship Troopers. How did you pull that off? We got our studio up and running digitally with Starship Troopers, and so quite a few members of the crew were fans of the show. I really banked on that. We were able to get a number of people to work on weekends or evenings, and that new crew of young guys made it possible. They really did a good job. What led you to score the movie in Moscow? That sounds quite grand. I've known the composers, John Morgan and Bill Stromberg, for many years. They primarily make their livings by doing reconstructions of old Max Steiner and Erich Kongold scores for the Marco Polo label. And because of Marco Polo's budgetary limitations, they have been recording in Moscow for the last ten or fifteen years. Bill was able to get a full orchestra for a billionth of the cost of doing it here in California. The score for this movie is very retro, with a lot of Bernard Herrmann and Max Steiner in the music. Are you pleased with the movie, overall? So far, yes. I was really lucky to bring in Louise as the editor because she's made sure I didn't look as stupid as I would have otherwise! Have you previewed it to friends? I showed it to Paul Verhoeven and Ed and a few key people here. You have to be careful about showing it to too many people. You need to have it critiqued by people who will tell you constructive things - not, I didn't like the main actors. What can you do about that? Would you ever consider directing a stop-motion animation feature? I have never even thought about it. I don't think it's remotely feasible - unless some great idea came along to make it so. Not even in the style of Henry Selick's work? Well, Henry does puppet films; I have a different style. I would be more inclined to develop a dramatic theatrical feature. But then I'd probably want to do it with computers. Any interest in directing commercials? No! I got started assisting David Allen on the Pillsbury Doughboy commercials at Cascade Pictures, with Dennis Muren, Ken Ralston and all those guys. After that, I realized that if I had to work with agency people again, I would probably be on Death Row. A technical question: Whatever happened to gomotion, the technology that enabled computerized rod puppets to be moved mechanically, then manipulated by hand in between frames? I think they melted it down and made anchors out of it for Navy ships! Go-motion was an interim idea - a bridge from Ray Harryhausen/Willis O'Brien stop-motion to computer graphics. Vermithrax Perjorative, the dragon in Dragonslayer, is still extremely impressive - wasn't that all go-motion? Yes, it was; but it took forever because we were developing the process, and computers were really weak at the time. It was so different from stop-motion. With most stop-motion performances, we ad-libbed. As long as we knew where we wanted to end up before we started, we could make things up as we went along. With go-motion, we had to previsualize everything, 100 percent, which was very convoluted and counter-intuitive. It was a little like computer animation today - we had to lay things in, bit by bit by bit. What do you look for in an animated character? What impresses you? A good character will appear to have its own motivation, on every level. If it looks like it weighs 125 pounds, then it moves like it's 125 pounds. A good character will appear to be a conscious entity that has a biological system for taking in information - and then it will do what it's supposed to do in the script. What animated characters have impressed you lately? I was really taken in by Gollum in The Lord of the Rings, like everybody was. But the filmmaking ideas were what interested me about that, not so much the technique. The performance was certainly fine; but the way that they expressed the schizophrenic side of the character, with the cutting, was brilliant because it told you so much about that guy. What are your feelings on advances in motion capture and how that applies to character animation? A technique is a technique. Whatever helps you to achieve the images you're looking for is fine, whether 20 • CINEFEX 97 it's a puppeteer moving a puppet, or an animator, or a performer. You just have to wire the technique into the appropriate context. You wouldn't want to animate a giant squid by putting a person in a bodysuit. That would be the wrong application. How do you feel about the use of artificial intelligence in animation? A.I. seems like a scary thing to be flirting with. I think that once A.I. programs become sufficiently developed, where people can set a couple of parameters and let shots run, then we'll be close to fulfilling the producer's hope in The Player - we'll be getting rid of the creative people and producing more 'stuff' without skill and craftsmanship. Generally, I think A.I. animation and procedural technology are all about trying to make things look real; and that is such a bogus, false economy. It's very easy to sell to people, because they're easily wowed by something that looks like a photograph that isn't a photograph. It's an impressive technical feat, but it doesn't mean anything. Do you still do any hands-on animation? Oh, no. I don't do that now. Do you sculpt or draw for your own pleasure? I do. What happens to that artwork? PaulVerhoeven - overshadowed by a full-scale cutout of prototype robotic law enforcement officer ED-209 - demonstrates a move for Tippett during the filming of RoboCop. Released in 1987, the darkly ironic science fiction tale kicked off a movie franchise that spawned two sequels and a television series, and initiated an enduring creative collaboration between Tippett, Verhoeven and producer Jon Davison. Tippett and his team provided stop-motion creations for all three RoboCop features, including the twitchy, but endearing ED-209, which wreaked havoc while delivering deadpan one-liners voiced by Jon Davison.

Tippett and computer systems lead Adam Valdez discuss the finer points of disemboweling a Ford Explorer for Jurassic Park. Credited as 'dinosaur supervisor, Tippett was originally engaged to supply go-motion animation for the landmark Steven Spielberg film, but eventually helped bridge the gap between the tactile realm and digital character animation produced at Tippett Studio and ILM. The project proved to be a watershed for all involved and for the visual effects industry in general, earning Tippett his second Oscar - following by ten years a special achievement award for Return I put it in a pile. A lot of times, I'll go to the art store and get a big ten-pound block of clay and put my hands in it, squish it, just for therapy. Do you still mine the fantasy vein in your personal No, not particularly. I have an education in so-called fine art. I draw all the time; sometimes it's representational, sometimes it's abstract. A lot of times I will do collages. One of my hobbies is to cut pictures out of magazines and categorize them - a bizarre obsession - and put them together in books. I have tons of giant books of images. It intrigues me, not working in a narrative context at all, putting pictures together that end up having some third meaning. For sculpting, I'll make a big pyramid out of clay, not fire it and take it in the backyard to watch it dissolve over a couple of years. It's nothing that I'd care to show. I've crossed paths with the art market, and it's as crazy as the movie market. Do you encourage your studio staff to take fine art courses, or acting lessons, like at Pixar where they have acting boot camps and seminars? We don't generally have the resources to do that, but we have tried to institute that from time to time on really tough projects. I certainly encourage it. All the key staff members have quite a bit of experience in filmmaking, sculpting or performance. But too many seminars can be dangerous. It's a little too 'ESTian,' I think, and it shows in the work. Aside from basic animation skills, what do you look for when you're hiring? Knowing something about film history is a huge help. I was appalled the other day - I was working on a scene at the end of Troopers 2, and I said, 'The energy here should be like the end scene in The Wild Bunch, where everybody's getting blown apart and blood is flying.' And many of the young guys in the crew asked, 'What's The Wild Bunch?' I was shocked! They didn't know! In order to communicate well, you have to be able to draw from every source - film history, art history. It's absolutely essential to have a knowledge of art history, so if someone is talking about Caravaggio or Rembrandt, you know the difference between the two. What do you look for in a visual effects supervisor? Again, the ability to communicate. Of course, the people that you've worked with the longest are always the people you communicate with the least because you are telepathically on the same wavelength. I can say to Eric, 'Hey, you know that thing with the thing that we did two years ago?' And he'll say, 'Oh, yeah, that one, right.' 'Well, we need a red one of those.'
